newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS - Polish finmin vows spending focus on flood.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Polish finmin vows spending focus on flood.

text.p: Polish Finance Minister Marek Belka vowed spending cuts in many areas next year to raise funds to rebuild areas devastated by July's flood without boosting inflation and jeopardising economic growth.

Belka said the flooding, which hit Poland more than three weeks ago causing billions of dollars of damage, had forced him to trim his earlier tentative spending proposals, because he did not want to abandon the bill's macroeconomic targets.

"This will be a budget of modest spending in many areas... and real wage increases will be limited next year," he told a news conference. He declined to give more details before cabinet debates on the budget, due later this month and in September.

The central bank meanwhile unveiled plans of increasing official interest rates within the next several weeks to prevent the dangerously booming credit action and domestic spending from accelerating even more because of the flood.

Belka said that while he understood the central bank's concerns, he thought the flood was unlikely to significantly slow down economic growth and create much inflationary pressure if public finances are kept tight, he said.
"The Polish economy is like a rushing locomotive, which the flood will not be able to stop," he told a news conference.

"There is a possiblity that in the first two months we will see a slow down because growth of industrial production will be somewhat smaller. But in a long-term perspective I foresee no statistically significant GDP slow down," he said.
He said he based his optimism on excellent revenues in July from the corporate tax, which would have been much worse had the flood caused significant damages in the economy.

Belka reaffirmed he would not drop his plan to cut the budget gap next year to 1.9 percent of gross domestic product from 2.8 percent planned for 1997 and curb inflation to less than 10 percent next year from June's 15.3 percent.

International financial organisations and the central bank have urged the government to propose an even smaller budget deficit to curb domestic demand, whose continued growth may hard hit the economy.

Belka said the ministry was considering introducing a special temporary tax next year to raise funds for the flood relief programme in the least pro-inflationary way. He declined to unveil the size of the tax, but said it should bring up to two billion zlotys ($576.7 million) in revenues in 1998.
Belka said he would prefer to impose the tax than to issue special tax-deductible bonds -- a measure proposed by the opposition, which the prime minister said would be taken into consideration.
"If I were to chose between a flood tax or a bond issue I would prefer the tax," Belka said. He added new bonds could discourage investors from buying the finance ministry's regular debt instruments.
The final decision on whether the government should ask parliament to impose the tax would be taken during the cabinet debates on next year's budget draft, he said.

Belka's plans, if they are adopted by the current government, can be changed by the next parliament that emerges from polls on September 21, which will pit the ruling ex-communists against right-leaning Solidarity Election Action alliance.
